input.content:
A Musical Journey

The History of Jazz

From the streets of New Orleans to the global stage — a century of improvisation, innovation, and cultural exchange.

02
The Roots

Blues, Ragtime & Rhythm

Late 19th century — American South

  • The Blues brought bent notes, call-and-response, and raw emotional storytelling.
  • Ragtime, popularized by Scott Joplin, gave jazz its syncopated, "ragged" rhythmic drive.
  • Brass bands, spirituals, work songs, and Caribbean rhythms formed a rich mix.
  • The "{{second line}}" parade beat of New Orleans laid the foundation for the groove.
03
The Birthplace

New Orleans: A Melting Pot

1880s – 1910s

  • A port city where African, European, and Caribbean traditions collided.
  • Congo Square hosted gatherings of drumming, dance, and song.
  • Early pioneers: Buddy Bolden, Jelly Roll Morton, and King Oliver.
  • Improvisation and collective interplay became the music's defining signature.
04
The Jazz Age

Jazz Goes Mainstream

The Roaring Twenties

  • Louis Armstrong revolutionized soloing with hot jazz and scat singing.
  • Jelly Roll Morton's Red Hot Peppers and Fletcher Henderson's orchestra shaped the big-band sound.
  • Prohibition-era speakeasies and dance halls spread the music nationwide.
  • The 1917 Original Dixieland Jass Band recordings carried jazz across the world.
05
The Big Band Era

Swing Takes Over

1930s – early 1940s

  • Big bands became the dominant force in popular music, built for dancing.
  • Giants: Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Benny Goodman, and Glenn Miller.
  • Arrangements pitted sections — reeds, brass, rhythm — against featured soloists.
  • Radio and film turned jazz into a mass-media phenomenon.
06
The Revolution

Bebop

Mid-1940s

  • A reaction against swing — music for listening, not dancing.
  • Lightning tempos, complex chord progressions, and virtuosic improvisation.
  • Charlie Parker (alto), Dizzy Gillespie (trumpet), and Thelonious Monk (piano) led the charge.
  • Born in the after-hours jam sessions of Harlem's Minton's Playhouse.
07
New Directions

Cool Jazz & Hard Bop

The 1950s

  • Cool jazz: relaxed and lyrical — Miles Davis's Birth of the Cool, the Dave Brubeck Quartet's "Take Five."
  • Hard bop: a return to blues and gospel roots — Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, Horace Silver.
  • Modal jazz: Davis's Kind of Blue (1959) traded chord changes for open scales.
  • Jazz became entwined with film noir and Beat-generation culture.
08
Breaking Boundaries

Free Jazz & the Avant-Garde

The 1960s

  • Ornette Coleman's Free Jazz (1960) abandoned fixed chord changes for collective improvisation.
  • John Coltrane's A Love Supreme brought spiritual depth and modal searching.
  • Cecil Taylor, Eric Dolphy, and Albert Ayler pushed the music to new extremes.
  • Shaped by the civil rights era and a drive for new forms of expression.
09
Electric & Beyond

Fusion & the Modern Era

1970s – today

  • Jazz-rock fusion added electric instruments and rock grooves — Davis's Bitches Brew, Weather Report, Herbie Hancock.
  • Jazz-funk, Latin jazz, and world music broadened the palette.
  • Wynton Marsalis and the repertory movement renewed interest in tradition.
  • Today's artists — Kamasi Washington, Esperanza Spalding, Robert Glasper — blend genres freely.
The Legacy

A Living, Breathing Art

  • Jazz is built on improvisation — individual voice in conversation with a community.
  • It shaped rock, hip-hop, R&B, and popular music around the world.
  • More than a genre, it is a universal language of freedom and expression.
"Jazz is the sound of freedom."
